entry.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
entry.content:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’

Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.

It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.

Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

entry.title: Collection of preserved UI style guides
entry.content:
Marcin Wichary

25 November 2026 / 69 style guides

UI style guides

This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

Amiga

(Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.

 Amiga User Interface Style Guide Android

Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

 Android Design Material Design v1 Material Design v2 Design for Android BlackBerry

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

 BlackBerry Wireless Handheld User Interface Style Guide BlackBerry PlayBook Tablet UI Guidelines BlackBerry Smartphones UI Guidelines BlackBerry 10 UI Guidelines CDE

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

 OSF/Motif Style Guide Common Desktop Environment: Style Guide and Certification Checklist CUA

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

 System Application Architecture: Common User Access Object-Oriented Interface Design: IBM Common User Access Guidelines GEM/TOS

Graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS.

 GEM User Interface Guidelines The documentation for TOS GNOME

GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

 GNOME Human Interface Guidelines GNOME Human Interface Guidelines GNOME Human Interface Guidelines iOS and iPadOS

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Appleâs mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

 iPhone Human Interface GuidelinesCovers the skeuomorphic era of iOS 1â6 iOS Human Interface GuidelinesCovers iOS 7+ iPad Human Interface Guidelines Apple Human Interface Guidelines Java

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

 Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines (2nd edition) Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines: Advanced Topics Macintosh

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the âclassicâ Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

 Apple Lisa Apple II Human Interface Guidelines Macintosh Human Interface Guidelines Mac OS 8 Human Interface Guidelines Mac

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

 Aqua Human Interface GuidelinesCovers early years of Aqua Apple Human Interface GuidelinesCovers evolving Aqua OS X Interface GuidelinesCovers the era between pure Aqua and Liquid Glass Apple Human Interface Guidelines Magic Cap

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.

 Magic Cap Concepts Microsoft Office

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.

 Microsoft Office System User Interface Design Guidelines NeXTSTEP

NeXTSTEP was NeXTâs influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

 NeXTstep Concepts NeXTSTEP User Interface Guidelines OpenStep User Interface Guidelines Newton

Apple Newton was Appleâs PDA launched in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

 Newton 2.0 User Interface Guidelines Nokia

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

 The User Interface of Nokia 9110 Communicator S60 UI Style Guide Symbian3 UI Style Guide Symbian Belle UI Style Guide OPEN LOOK

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

 OPEN LOOK: Graphical User Interface Functional Specification OPEN LOOK: Graphical User Interface Application Style Guidelines Palm OS

Palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palmâs mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.

 Palm OS User Interface Guidelines Zen of Palm PenPoint

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

 PenPoint UI Design Guidelines RISC OS

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

 RISC OS Style Guide Samsung

Various Samsung style guides.

 The Samsung Gear UI Design Guidelines One UI Design Guidelines Samsung Smart TV Design Guides Silicon Graphics

Style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

 SGI Indigo Magic User Interface Guidelines SGI IRIX Interactive Desktop User Interface Guidelines Taligent

Taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

 Human Interface Guidelines webOS

webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

 Palm webOS User Interface Design Guidelines Palm Design Guide HP Touchpad webOS Design Guidelines Windows

Does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

 Microsoft Windows Software Development Kit Application Style Guide The Windows Interface: An Application Design Guide The Windows Interface Guidelines for Software Design Microsoft Windows User Experience:Â Official Guidelines for User Interface Developers and Designers User Experience â Official Guidelines for User Interface Developers and Designers Windows XP Visual Guidelines Windows 8â10 User Experience Guidelines Design basics for Windows apps Windows Phone

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6, and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

 Designing Applications for Windows Mobile Powered Platforms UI Design and Interaction Guide for Windows Phone 7

Thatâs it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

Some of the above mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier â stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds.

You can also download all the above style guides in one archive.

entry.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
entry.content:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.

minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.

The demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.

The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.

minipg app.pgdb # psql shell (creates app.pgdb if missing) minipg app.pgdb "select 1" # one statement minipg url app.pgdb # postgres://postgres:...@127.0.0.1:54321/app minipg serve app.pgdb # an explicit foreground server minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start # your app, with DATABASE_URL set minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql # and minipg restore app.pgdb dump.sql

A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.

In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:

minipg init test.pgdb minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...

The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.

Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.

Linux x86_64 KVM, or h9's native backend without it (Linux 5.11 or later) Linux arm64 KVM macOS (Apple Silicon) Hypervisor.framework The browser h9's web host, v86, and minipg's Linux build

The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:

git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg cd minipg make build # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg make root ARCH=386 make web # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web

minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.

Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.

entry.title: Unconditional Integer Factorization in Subexponential Time
entry.content:
This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine $\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization $N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$) of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$, where

$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$

and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means

$$ \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c. $$

Every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$, with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0) formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released in a companion submission.

This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. There was no human interaction other than the initial prompt for Cogentic to generate a full proof and formalization. The Cogentic harness was built by Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, and Di Wang (Google Research and Google DeepMind).

entry.title: Lions' Commentary on Unix: Why It Was Secretly Copied for 20 Years
entry.content:
17. Lions' Commentary on Unix Lions' Commentary on Unix

John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.

What's the best way toteach operating systems?

They need to study the Unix source.But it's tough going.

I'll write myown textbook.

In May 1976, Lions prepared lecture notes explaining the kernel source code of AT&T's Unix Version 6. These became his Unix commentary.

To understand an OS,we need to readthe actual code.

I've written a guideto the Unix kernel.We'll use it asour textbook.

By 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].

Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].

I am altering the license.Pray I don't alter itany further.

Destroy Lions' book.No more teachingUnix source code.

There is no escapefrom our operating system.

He's teaching from the Unix source code!Seize the books!Run!

He's got the book!

Don't let himescape!

Quick! Takethe book!

Ugh!

I find your interestin source code disturbing.

Just use the system calls.Learn a little theory.Leave the internals to us.

Theory isn't enough.I need to see the code.

This code is our only hopeof understanding an OS.

For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].

Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].

Lions' book is finallyin print. It even hasmy foreword.

People were secretly copying itfor twenty years?Unbelievable.

You can read a reconstructed version of the commentary as a PDF, or order a print copy on Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code is available separately from TUHS.

References Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code John Lions, Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code, Peer-to-Peer Communications, 1996 (ISBN 1-57398-013-7). System call UNIX News, Vol. 2 No. 3, March 1977 - John Lions's March 11, 1977 letter and the announcement of book distribution to Unix licensees. Rachel Chalmers, "Code critic", Salon, November 30, 1999 - recollections from students and Dennis Ritchie, distribution restrictions, and the path to publication. Peter H. Salus, The Daemon, the GNU and the Penguin, Chapter 6: "1979", 2005 - the Version 7 license terms announced at USENIX in June 1979 and restrictions on classroom use. Dennis Ritchie's October 22, 1995 letter and Peter H. Salus's July 12, 1996 letter - publication-permission correspondence preserved by Warren Toomey. MIT, "Xv6, a simple Unix-like teaching operating system", "History and Background" - teaching with Lions's commentary and the background to xv6.

entry.title: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
entry.content:
High Energy Physics - Theory

[Submitted on 25 Nov 2026]

Title:An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null coneView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory. Submission historyFrom: Venkatesa Chandrasekaran [view email]

entry.title: Intel One Mono font
entry.content:
Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use. The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps. The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.

We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:

Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03: Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature. Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4. Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates). Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results. Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs/sinf (Subscript) features. Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:

VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'" Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:

For .otf builds, we recommend activating “Decompose” as well as “Autohint” options. For .ttf, .woff and .woff2 builds, we recommend activating the “Autohint” option only (see note on hinting below). In any case, we recommend using the “Release Mode” setting for best results.

If you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare new interpolations to the existing instance sources and update them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

For TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open issues and we will try to accomodate them.

NP_R ≠ PAR_R
entry.content:
Important

Motivated by the recent breakthrough on the VP vs VNP problem, the authors (Samuel Everett and Deven Mithal) guided instances of ChatGPT and Claude to develop further, more granular algebraic complexity class separations. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Sam and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote most of the paper under his guidance. That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP}{\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR}{\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below. All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind.

In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of

NP_ℝ and coNP_ℝ, the second existential level Σ₂ of the real polynomial hierarchy, constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs with real messages, interactive proofs with Boolean messages (BIP_ℝ),

and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ).

Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$, also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph.

The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound:

the graph theorems: a polynomial of polynomial degree whose graph has short existential, universal or ∃∀ real certificates has small border complexity; AM_ℝ[O(1)] = NP_ℝ ⊊ AM_ℝ[poly]. File Content main.tex Title, abstract, section includes macros.tex Notation refs.bib Bibliography sections/intro.tex Introduction and statements of the main theorems sections/prelim.tex Model, classes, border complexity, semialgebraic tools, cells sections/core.tex Derivatives of semialgebraic families, Newton iteration as a circuit, the local theorem sections/certificates.tex Existential certificates: graph theorem, thresholds, value functions sections/universal.tex Universal certificates and the complex field sections/second-level.tex An existential and a universal block sections/interaction.tex Boolean messages and constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs sections/open.tex Open problems sections/lean.tex Appendix A: the Lean formalization, with the correspondence between results and Lean theorems lean/ The Lean 4 formalization (see lean/README.md)
latexmk -pdf main.tex

The directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it:

cd lean lake exe cache get lake build

Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result.

The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms:

SAFacts — facts (S2)–(S8) on semialgebraic sets; PermLowerBound — Theorem 2.3, the border-complexity lower bound for the permanent; BurgisserThm — Theorem 2.5; EffectiveQE — effective quantifier elimination [BPR06]; CountingBound — the counting bound (C) of Lemma 7.7; ClassFacts — the known inclusions between complexity classes.

In particular, every separation is conditional on PermLowerBound, exactly as in the paper.

Fact (S1) holds by construction: semialgebraic sets are defined as first-order definable sets. Baur–Strassen, Ryser's formula, Hoeffding's inequality (from Mathlib) and the unrolling of machines into trees are proved.

Appendix A of the paper (sections/lean.tex) and lean/README.md list the Lean name of each result, the modelling choices, and the few places where a formal proof differs from the text. lean/ClassSeparations/Pinned.lean restates the main statements verbatim and checks them against the proved theorems.

The proofs have not been peer reviewed. The paper is mostly AI-written (see above). The results are formalized in Lean, conditional on the cited results listed above.

The bibliographic data in refs.bib were checked against publisher and Crossref records. The numbered results cited from the Anthropic manuscript, Bürgisser (2004, 2026), Baartse–Meer, Baur–Strassen and Cucker et al. were confirmed in the sources. Still to be confirmed against the full texts: the attributions to Cucker (1992, 1993), Koiran (1994), Blum–Cucker–Shub–Smale, and the numbering in Basu–Pollack–Roy, which follows the second edition (2006).

Tracking Diseases Cured by AI
entry.content:
A public ledger — updated when the number changes Last checked · Nov 26, 2026

Number of diseases cured by AI

0

Diseases cured Verified · FDA / EMA approvals Est. forever ago

Zero. Not “almost one.” Not “one, if you count a scan.” No disease has been cured by a cure that AI discovered — no AI-discovered drug has even been approved yet.

Snapshot as of Nov 26, 2026 — checked against FDA approvals through November 2026. This page does not poll live.

1,452 days since ChatGPT launched 1,452 of those days at zero $6.93B AI drug-discovery market in 2025 — and counting

0

Diseases cured by an AI-discovered treatment. The whole point of this page.

0

AI-discovered drugs approved by the FDA or EMA. None, as of Nov 2026.

117

AI-enabled candidates that had entered human trials by July 2025, from 63 companies.

1

Reached Phase III. Rentosertib for lung fibrosis — still investigational, not a cure.

What would actually move this to 1?

The bar is not mysterious. It is the same bar every other drug has to clear. AI does not get a discount for being exciting in a keynote.

Counts All three have to be true ✓AI found it. The target and the molecule were both chosen or designed by AI — not just “AI was used somewhere in the building.” ✓Regulators approved it. It finished Phase III and was approved by the FDA, EMA, or an equivalent regulator for that disease. ✓It cures. Patients are cured — disease eliminated or durably reversed — not just symptoms managed a little better for a little longer. Doesn’t count Impressive ≠ a cure ×Reading a scan. 1,614 AI devices are FDA-authorized, mostly for radiology. Detecting is not curing. ×Predicting a protein. AlphaFold is a genuine breakthrough. A predicted shape is not a treated patient. ×Still in a trial. Phase I, II, or III is a promise with paperwork. This counter only moves on approval + cure. ×Helping in the lab. Faster screening, better papers, cheaper discovery — valuable, and still not a cure. Closest to breaking the zero

If the number ever changes, it will almost certainly start here. None of these is there yet — here is exactly how far each one is.

01

Rentosertib — Insilico Medicine · idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The furthest along by a clear margin, and the first drug where AI picked both the target (TNIK) and the molecule. Phase IIa in Nature Medicine (71 patients, 12 weeks) showed a +98.4 mL lung-function signal at the top dose. Phase III started in 2026 — 320 patients, 52 weeks. IPF has no cure today; even success here would first be a treatment, not yet a cure.

Phase III · started Sep 9, 2026First patient dosedReadout still ahead

Distance to 1

Phase III → ?

02

Zasocitinib — Takeda / Nimbus · psoriasis

The nearest FDA decision: the FDA accepted its application with a target date in Q1 2027 after it beat an approved rival in Phase III. The catch for this counter: its roots are physics-based modelling from around 2016 against an already-known target, and psoriasis treatment is management, not a cure.

NDA under Priority ReviewDecision due Q1 2027Treats, does not cure

Distance to 1

Filed, not cured

03

Isomorphic Labs — Alphabet / DeepMind spinout

The loudest promise and the thinnest clinical record. Raised $2.1B in May 2026 on the strength of AlphaFold. As of November 2026, no Isomorphic molecule had been dosed in a human — first-in-human was targeted for the end of 2026.

$2.1B Series B · May 2026No human dosing yetNo named candidate disclosed

Distance to 1

Pre-clinical

The promises this counter is measured against

The people selling AI have put a timeline on curing disease. These are their words, verbatim. The zero above is the score so far.

If today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade.

Dario Amodei

CEO of Anthropic · Anthropic IPO roadshow video · November 10, 2026

We will see diseases get cured at an unprecedented rate. We will be amazed at how quickly we're curing this cancer and that one, and heart disease.

Sam Altman

CEO of OpenAI · Stargate announcement at the White House · January 21, 2025

I think one day, maybe we can cure all diseases with the help of AI. I think that's within reach. Maybe within the next decade or so, I don't see why not.

Demis Hassabis

CEO of Google DeepMind · CBS 60 Minutes · April 2025

I believe AI has the potential to cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.

Bill Gates

Co-founder of Microsoft and chair of the Gates Foundation · X · November 20, 2026

entry.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Bypass anti-adblock
entry.content:
Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

YouTube serves an ad roughly every 60 seconds. You can't watch one minute of content without being interrupted by a commercial. Traditional ad blockers get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"). Skip buttons take 5 seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

 Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume ↓ (if 3 reloads fail) Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping)

Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default.

Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver)

Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage

Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL

Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes

Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops

 ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles) ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve) ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs, only on YouTube domains Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git Open chrome://extensions Enable Developer mode (top right) Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested

Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):

In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs, and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load

Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

 Download the latest release from Releases Unzip and follow Option A steps 2–5

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:

Field What it captures Timestamp When the ad was detected Advertiser Company name from the ad overlay Video Title of the video you were watching Video time Your playback position before reload Ad duration Length of the ad Skip text "Skip Ad" button text (if available) Action Reloaded or skipped

Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

If millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator

 Tool How it works Reloads? Collects data? uBlock Origin Blocks ad network requests No No SponsorBlock Skips sponsored segments in videos No No Enhancer for YouTube Auto-clicks "Skip Ad" button No No 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher Detects ad → reloads → seeks to timestamp Yes Yes Popup blockers Block window.open() popups No No

Best combo: uBlock Origin (blocks most ads) + 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher (catches the ones that slip through and logs them) + SponsorBlock (skips sponsor reads). They don't conflict.

YouTube changes DOM class names periodically — if ads aren't detected, check the console for [YT-AdReloader] logs Some ads (mid-roll on live streams) can't preserve position — plain reload YouTube's "Premium" upsell interstitials may need a second reload cycle (handled by cooldown) File Purpose manifest.json Chrome extension manifest v3 content.js Ad detection + reload + timestamp restore + history tracking popup.html / popup.js Ad history viewer with export background.js Minimal service worker

MIT — do whatever you want with it.

Built with Alice (SIFTA) for George Anton.

"If millions installed this, YouTube would feel every reload." 🐜

entry.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' Indicted for Wire Fraud
entry.content:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
